newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA GOLD - HEDGING TAPERS OFF BUT STILL KEY.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA GOLD - HEDGING TAPERS OFF BUT STILL KEY.

text.p: Hedging activity in the Australian gold market, one of the world's most robust, has eased in recent weeks, although mining companies continue to focus on protection against their mining costs.
Bullion dealers and corporate financial advisers point to hefty long-term gold lease rates as an indication that hedging remains an active component of the gold market.
Mining companies in Australia, the world's third larget producer, have been big hedgers in the market for years.

Unlike in some other gold-producing centres, such as North America, lending institutions encourage and sometimes require Australian mining houses to hedge large portions of their future yields to reduce exposure to volatility in the market.
The 12-month lease rate, which typically averages about 1.5 percent annually, currently hovers at 2.10 percent, pointing to demand for metal to cover hedges.
Long term rates moved significantly in the days following announcement by Australia's Reserve Bank on July 4 that it had sold 167 tonnes or two-thirds of its gold.
The RBA move had a two-tiered effect on the market -- driving metals prices down but also pushing up lease rates as the bank was in effect "factored out" of the supply side.

Brokerage Hartley Poynton Ltd calculates that Australian miners on average hedged 197 tonnes of gold a year between 1986 and 1996, which is roughly two-thirds of the forecast total production for Australia this year.
In light of the RBA sales and rising production costs among many of the miners, this figure could be higher in 1997.
"Certainly in the days since the sales, our mining clients have been very interested in increasing their protection," a gold dealer in Sydney said.
But this is not to suggest there is little business taking place in the spot market, where lease rates of about 1.80 percent also are high on an historical basis.
"With short-term lease rates what you're looking at is more spot activity," said a bullion dealer.
Typically if investors are shorting gold, short-term lease rates go up because of a rise in borrowed gold to cover the positions.
